marrow__ANAT_CH50_Q015.takeaway: The marked visceral impression on the spleen is the left kidney impression.
marrow__ANAT_CH50_Q015.displayText:
The marked visceral impression on the spleen is the left kidney impression.

The area marked on the visceral surface of the spleen is related to the left kidney.

The source figure shows the gastric, pancreatic, colic and renal impressions on the visceral surface of the spleen.
emphasis: The marked visceral impression on the spleen is the left kidney impression

rationales.a: Gastric impression is anteromedial rather than the labeled posterior renal impression.
rationales.b: Pancreatic tail contacts the hilum but is a distinct impression.
rationales.c: Colic impression is inferior and smaller.

marrow__ANAT_CH50_Q016.takeaway: The splenic artery is ligated at the splenorenal ligament, which carries splenic vessels and pancreatic tail toward the spleen.
marrow__ANAT_CH50_Q016.displayText:
The splenic artery is ligated at the splenorenal ligament, which carries splenic vessels and pancreatic tail toward the spleen.

The splenorenal ligament contains the splenic artery. Therefore, during splenectomy, it is ligated at the splenorenal ligament.

The source table summarizes splenic ligaments, attachments, and contents.
emphasis: The splenic artery is ligated at the splenorenal ligament, which carries splenic vessels and pancreatic tail toward the spleen

rationales.a: Gastrosplenic ligament carries short gastric and left gastroepiploic vessels, not the main splenic artery.
rationales.b: Splenocolic ligament is not the principal vascular pedicle.
rationales.d: Phrenicosplenic ligament is an attachment, not the vessel-bearing splenic pedicle.

marrow__ANAT_CH50_Q017.takeaway: The phrenicocolic ligament supports the spleen inferiorly and limits its descent toward the left iliac fossa.
marrow__ANAT_CH50_Q017.displayText:
The phrenicocolic ligament supports the spleen inferiorly and limits its descent toward the left iliac fossa.

Downward displacement of the spleen towards the left iliac fossa is prevented by the phrenicocolic ligament. Therefore the spleen usually enlarges towards the right iliac fossa.

The phrenicocolic ligament connects the splenic flexure of the colon to the diaphragm. It is not attached to the spleen, but lies below it and supports its lower pole. When the spleen gets enlarged, the phrenicocolic ligament along with the splenic flexure restricts its downward displacement.

The phrenicocolic ligament functions as a potential barrier to spread of infection between the left paracolic gutter and the left subphrenic space.
emphasis: The phrenicocolic ligament supports the spleen inferiorly and limits its descent toward the left iliac fossa

rationales.a: Splenorenal ligament carries splenic vessels but does not form the inferior shelf.
rationales.c: The left kidney is posterior to the spleen and does not provide the named inferior support.
rationales.d: Gastrosplenic ligament attaches spleen to stomach and carries short gastric vessels.

marrow__ANAT_CH50_Q018.takeaway: A pancreatic-head tumor extending posteriorly can involve the right renal vein behind the head/uncinate region.
marrow__ANAT_CH50_Q018.displayText:
A pancreatic-head tumor extending posteriorly can involve the right renal vein behind the head/uncinate region.

The right renal vein forms a posterior relation of the head of the pancreas, so it may be invaded by posterior expansion of a carcinoma of the head of the pancreas.

Posterior relations of the head include right renal vein, right renal artery, inferior vena cava, common bile duct embedded in the head, right crus of the diaphragm, and termination of the right gonadal vein. Anterior relations include the first part of the duodenum and origin of the transverse mesocolon.

Relations of the neck: anteriorly the lesser sac, pylorus, and anterior superior pancreaticoduodenal branch of the gastroduodenal artery; posteriorly the portal vein, superior mesenteric vein, and inferior mesenteric vein in about one-third of individuals.

Clinical note: Cancers arising from the head or neck of the pancreas are difficult to operate on because of the confluence of so many vessels near them; this also makes blood-borne spread faster.
emphasis: A pancreatic-head tumor extending posteriorly can involve the right renal vein behind the head/uncinate region

rationales.b: Transverse colon is anterior/inferior to pancreas, not the posterior extension target.
rationales.c: Aorta is posterior but the source-keyed adjacent vessel is right renal vein.
rationales.d: Lesser sac lies anterior to pancreas.

marrow__ANAT_CH50_Q019.takeaway: The major duodenal papilla receives the hepatopancreatic ampulla; the source figure labels ampulla as A.
marrow__ANAT_CH50_Q019.displayText:
The major duodenal papilla receives the hepatopancreatic ampulla; the source figure labels ampulla as A.

The structure marked A in the image is the Ampulla of Vater.

The bile duct and pancreatic duct unite to form the hepatopancreatic ampulla (ampulla of Vater) within the second part of the duodenum, which opens at the major duodenal papilla.

Sometimes an accessory pancreatic duct is present and opens into the minor duodenal papilla, about 2 cm proximal to the major duodenal papilla in the second part of the duodenum.

Clinical note: Familial adenomatous polyposis (APC gene defect) is associated with carcinoma of the Ampulla of Vater. Duodenal villous adenomas are commonly found around the ampulla and may be premalignant. Duodenal injuries with tissue loss distal to the major duodenal papilla and proximal to the superior mesenteric vessels are best treated in the source note by Roux-en-Y duodenojejunostomy.
emphasis: The major duodenal papilla receives the hepatopancreatic ampulla; the source figure labels ampulla as A

rationales.b: Label B marks a different structure in the duodenal diagram, not the ductal confluence.
rationales.c: Label C is not the ampullary junction identified at the major papilla.
rationales.d: Label D does not indicate the confluence of bile and pancreatic ducts.

marrow__ANAT_CH50_Q020.takeaway: The pancreas is secondarily retroperitoneal, so its posterior surface is not covered by peritoneum; the tail is an exception.
marrow__ANAT_CH50_Q020.displayText:
The pancreas is secondarily retroperitoneal, so its posterior surface is not covered by peritoneum; the tail is an exception.

The entire posterior surface of the pancreas is devoid of peritoneum.

The posterior surface lies over the fascia of Toldt in front of the aorta. The splenic vein traverses directly on this surface.

Only parts of the uncinate process where the superior mesenteric vessels descend on it are also devoid of peritoneum. The entire anterior surface of the body is covered by peritoneum and the tail lies between layers of the splenorenal ligament, which is formed from peritoneum.

Note that the pancreas is a retroperitoneal organ except for the tail; in that sense it is not enveloped by peritoneum, but the anterior surface is in contact with peritoneum.
emphasis: The pancreas is secondarily retroperitoneal, so its posterior surface is not covered by peritoneum; the tail is an exception

rationales.a: The tail lies in the splenorenal ligament and is intraperitoneal.
rationales.b: The tail is peritoneal-covered, so the entire pancreas is not devoid of peritoneum.
rationales.c: The anterior surface is covered by peritoneum bordering the lesser sac.

marrow__ANAT_CH50_Q021.takeaway: Pancreatic arterial supply derives from celiac-trunk and SMA branches, including splenic, gastroduodenal and pancreaticoduodenal arteries.
marrow__ANAT_CH50_Q021.displayText:
Pancreatic arterial supply derives from celiac-trunk and SMA branches, including splenic, gastroduodenal and pancreaticoduodenal arteries.

The arterial supply of the pancreas is mainly by branches of the coeliac trunk and the superior mesenteric artery.

Arterial supply includes anterior and posterior superior pancreaticoduodenal arteries (branches of the gastroduodenal artery, itself a branch of the coeliac trunk); anterior and posterior inferior pancreaticoduodenal arteries (branches of the inferior pancreaticoduodenal artery from the superior mesenteric artery); body and tail branches of the splenic artery; dorsal pancreatic artery; great pancreatic artery; and artery to the tail of the pancreas.

Options A and C include branches of the coeliac trunk but do not include branches from the superior mesenteric artery, so they are incomplete. Right gastric and right renal arteries do not supply the pancreas.
emphasis: Pancreatic arterial supply derives from celiac-trunk and SMA branches, including splenic, gastroduodenal and pancreaticoduodenal arteries

rationales.a: Celiac trunk alone omits inferior pancreaticoduodenal supply from SMA.
rationales.b: Right gastric and renal arteries are not the main pancreatic arterial sources.
rationales.c: These are relevant arteries but omit the SMA contribution to pancreatic head.

marrow__ANAT_CH50_Q022.takeaway: The uncinate process passes posterior to the superior mesenteric vessels, so a tumor there can involve the SMA.
marrow__ANAT_CH50_Q022.displayText:
The uncinate process passes posterior to the superior mesenteric vessels, so a tumor there can involve the SMA.

A tumor of the uncinate process of the pancreas affects the superior mesenteric artery.

The superior mesenteric artery arises from the abdominal aorta. It lies first behind the body of the pancreas and then in front of the uncinate process.

The source repeats relations of the pancreatic head and neck, including the portal and superior mesenteric veins posterior to the neck.
emphasis: The uncinate process passes posterior to the superior mesenteric vessels, so a tumor there can involve the SMA

rationales.b: Portal vein forms behind the pancreatic neck and is less directly related to the uncinate process.
rationales.c: Common hepatic artery courses superiorly, away from the uncinate’s close relation.
rationales.d: Inferior mesenteric artery is not adjacent to the pancreatic uncinate process.

marrow__ANAT_CH50_Q023.takeaway: Image 3 shows pancreas divisum, with failure of dorsal and ventral pancreatic ducts to fuse.
marrow__ANAT_CH50_Q023.displayText:
Image 3 shows pancreas divisum, with failure of dorsal and ventral pancreatic ducts to fuse.

Pancreas divisum has been depicted in the image marked 3.

The pancreas has two ducts that normally fuse during embryological development. The accessory (dorsal) pancreatic duct of Santorini drains the upper part of the anterior portion of the pancreatic head. The main pancreatic duct of Wirsung usually runs within the substance of the gland from left to right.

When the ventral and dorsal ducts fail to fuse, pancreas divisum results. In this condition, most of the pancreas drains through a dominant dorsal duct that enters the duodenum at the minor papilla. A short ventral duct, along with the bile duct, drains to the major duodenal papilla. Therefore, major pancreatic drainage is via the dorsal duct, which opens at the minor papilla.

Patients are usually asymptomatic; however, 25-28% of these patients may experience recurrent pancreatitis that may progress to chronic pancreatitis.

Image A shows normal pancreatic ducts with communication between main and accessory ducts. Image B shows normal pancreatic ducts with no communication between main and accessory ducts. Image D shows absence of the accessory pancreatic duct.
emphasis: Image 3 shows pancreas divisum, with failure of dorsal and ventral pancreatic ducts to fuse

rationales.a: Image 1 shows a normal ductal pattern with duct communication.
rationales.b: Image 2 shows normal ducts without the divisum arrangement as described by the source.
rationales.d: Image 4 shows absence of accessory duct rather than unfused dorsal and ventral systems.
